fetched_contents.text: Why do we use Lactulose and Rifaximin for Hepatic Encephalopathy? Lactulose and Rifaximin (Xifaxan) are standards of care for the prevention of overt hepatic encephalopathy in patients with cirrhosis. Have you ever wondered why? Join us! First, if you want a refresher on hepatic encephalopathy (HE), check out our “Quick Tips” post by Lizzie Aby. What is the first step in treating HE? Reverse the underlying cause!!! Infections, GI bleeding, medications, and dehydration can precipitate HE and treating these factors is most important in reversing an acute episode of HE. So what next? Medical therapy! Lactulose, a non-absorbable sugar composed of galactose and glucose was first made in 1929. It was first used in 1966 by Bircher et al. to treat HE: In this case report, the authors describe the proposed mechanism of action for the drug: “The non-absorbed lactulose passes intact into the ascending colon, where it is split by bacterial action into lower molecular organic acids (mainly lactic acid and acetic acid). Their osmotic effect creates a “fermentive diarrhea” identical to the lactose-induced diarrhea in lactase-deficient subjects. The lowered fecal pH caused by the presence of these organic acids should hypothetically entail a change in colonic bacterial flora or a change in bacterial metabolism. An increase in fermentation and a decrease in putrefaction is to be expected; this should decrease the amount of nitrogenous compounds which are “toxic” in the portal-systemic encephalopathy.” Another study published in 1969 by Elkington et al. further elucidated the mechanism of lactulose therapy. In this study, 10 patients with HE, all of whom had been treated by dietary protein restriction and prolonged administration of neomycin, were treated with lactulose or sorbitol (an osmotic laxative) and then were crossed over. The authors found that HE that was observed on sorbitol could be reversed by lactulose. Though both drugs are laxatives, the difference was that lactulose lowered stool pH! As it turns out, not much has changed in terms of our understanding of the mechanism of the drug. It is thought to reduce the intestinal production/absorption of ammonia by several mechanisms: 1. Colonic breakdown of lactulose to lactic acid leads to acidification of the gut which favors the formation of nonabsorbable NH4+ from NH3, thereby trapping NH4+ in the colon and reducing plasma ammonia concentrations. 2. Colonic acidification displaces urease-producing bacteria with non-urease producing Lactobacillus. 3. Lactulose works as a cathartic agent with a hyperosmolar load, leading to frequent bowel movements, with less time for ammonia absorption and increased fecal nitrogen excretion. 4. Lactulose can have a prebiotic effect even at low doses by increasing the relative amount of bifidobacterial and lactobacilli and decreased branched-chain fatty acids. 5. Lactulose can decrease bacterial-DNA translocation, perhaps by accelerating intestinal transit and improving bacterial overgrowth and intestinal permeability. One of the first trials of lactulose was published in Gastroenterology in 1970 by Simmons et al. In this double-blind clinical trial, 11 patients with HE received 80g of lactulose daily while 10 patients received 60g of glucose daily as a control. Patients receiving lactulose demonstrated a significant reduction in HE and blood ammonia levels compared to controls. Interestingly, several patients dropped out of the study and the final analysis included only 4 patients in the lactulose group and 10 in the control group. In a recent meta-analysis and systematic review, lactulose was found to prevent the risk of developing serious liver-related adverse events and reduces mortality. Because of these studies and because of its success in clinical practice, lactulose is currently considered to be the “gold standard” for the treatment of acute episodes of hepatic encephalopathy. In the acute setting, lactulose is usually given until encephalopathy begins to improve. If the patient is able to swallow, it is administered orally, but it can also be administered via OG or NG tube, as well as rectally. Once acute encephalopathy is resolved, lactulose is given to target 2-3 bowel movements per day. Lactulose is associated with several side effects, however, that make it intolerable to many patients. Because it is non-absorbable, it can be associated with flatulence, abdominal discomfort, bloating, and diarrhea. In patients with cirrhosis who are already quite sick and prone to electrolyte abnormalities, excessive diarrhea caused by lactulose can exacerbate hypokalemia and lead to hypernatremia. Additionally, because of the frequency of bowel movements that lactulose causes, some patients may experience perianal irritation. Because of these side effects, many patients are unable to be compliant with lactulose therapy. Patient compliance may also be impacted by socio-cultural factors as well as its perceived benefits. So doc, what else can I use for an acute episode of HE? Given that the pathophysiology of lactulose is at least partly based on the displacement of urease-producing bacteria, several oral antibiotics (neomycin, paromomycin, vancomycin, and metronidazole) have been studied based on their ability to similarly reduce ammonia-producing enteric bacteria. Most of these antibiotics when taken long-term, however, are associated with side effects, including nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, and peripheral neuropathy. Additionally, taking systemic antibiotics long-term can be associated with antibiotic resistance, and remember, we are talking about a population that is already prone to infection and resistant organisms. Published in final edited form as: Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2022 Aug;20(8 Suppl):S20–S29. doi: 10.1016/j.cgh.2022.04.035 Abstract As the world’s population ages, diseases predominantly found in the elderly now overlap with diseases that were thought to be the purview of younger patients. This includes chronic liver disease (CLD), which affects more than 2 billion people worldwide1. Due to the obesity epidemic (and associated metabolic diseases), nonalcoholic fatty liver disease has become the most common cause of CLD and cirrhosis2. A major complication of cirrhosis is hepatic encephalopathy (HE), which becomes challenging to diagnose in elderly patients3. HE is usually included in the differential diagnosis of acute delirium, but not of reversible dementias. To illustrate this point, we present two cases of older patients that were misdiagnosed as having dementia and Parkinson’s disease or a parkinsonian syndrome but had contributions from cirrhosis. Both cognitive impairment and tremor resolved with treatment of HE. Keywords: Dementia, Parkinson’s disease, Wernicke’s encephalopathy, Alcohol, Lewy Body Dementia, Progressive Supranuclear palsy, EncephalApp Case 1 A 71-year-old male with hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, non-alcoholic cirrhosis, and thalamic and basal ganglia infarcts presented with tremor, shuffling gait, orthostatic symptoms, and memory issues. On exam, he was alert and oriented, with intact recent and remote memory, but bradyphrenia noted. No signs of asterixis were observed. Working diagnosis was vascular Parkinsonism, versus other parkinsonian syndrome, including multi system atrophy with predominant Parkinsonism, (MSA-P). He was started on a trial of carbidopa/levodopa. At follow-up, patient reported no improvement in symptoms and therefore he was titrated off carbidopa-levodopa. One month later, patient reported worsened memory and onset of visual hallucinations, at that time symptoms did not seem consistent with hepatic encephalopathy given the predominant motor symptoms, intact alertness and orientation and worsened delayed memory. A few months later, he returned with worsening confusion including putting his clothes on backwards, not recognizing eating utensils, and urinating on bathroom floor. Per caregiver, some days he was better, others worse. Mental status exam revealed that while oriented to name and place, he did not know the month, his age, or date of birth. He also had difficulty following simple commands. Lewy body dementia (LBD) was on top of the differential because of fluctuation of symptoms, vs. vascular dementia. As the patient reported 2–3 bowel movements daily on psyllium and polyethylene glycol, HE was not a major concern. Two weeks later he presented to the ER with abdominal pain and increased confusion. Labs showed leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, elevated liver function tests, and ammonia level >100. CT showed cholelithiasis without ductal dilatation. Cultures were negative. He was diagnosed with sepsis possibly due to intra-abdominal infection and acute hepatic encephalopathy. Treatment included lactulose and rifaximin. Three months later, patient and caregiver reported that his symptoms (memory loss, hallucinations, falls and tremor) resolved after starting lactulose and rifaximin. On exam he was alert and oriented x4, recent and remote memory were intact, attention, concentration and serial 3’s were normal. His wife noted: “He is a different person!”. Case 2 73-year-old male with hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, anemia, tremor, history of alcohol abuse (quit 2 years prior) and head trauma from boxing presented to ER with history of fever, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, confusion, and fall resulting in head laceration. He was alert and oriented with normal neurologic exam but had amnesia of the fall and injury. Labs showed normocytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, hyperbilirubinemia, normal AST, ALT and ammonia, and negative urine drug and alcohol screen. Head CT with chronic microvascular ischemic changes frontal lobes. Ultrasound showed cholelithiasis and liver nodularity. He was discharged the next day. Four months later, patient admitted from an assisted living facility with increased confusion and difficulty ambulating. Labs included elevated creatinine and BUN, hyperbilirubinemia, thrombocytopenia, and prolonged INR. AST and ALT normal. Head CT without acute pathology. CT abdomen showed gallstone and nodular liver. Diagnoses included metabolic encephalopathy, acute kidney injury due to poor oral intake combined with ACEI and HCTZ, urinary retention, possible Parkinson’s disease, and dementia. Treatment included intravenous fluids, tamsulosin, donepezil and carbidopa-levodopa. Patient transferred to skilled nursing facility (SNF). On exam, disoriented to time and place, without focal neurologic deficits. Labs remarkable for ammonia 114, elevated lactate, and thrombocytopenia. Head CT was unchanged. ## Laboratory interpretation and implications for cirrhosis management

The provided lab values—**RBC 3.9, HGB 11.2, albumin 2.1**—are consistent with several important cirrhosis-related abnormalities. In cirrhosis, hypoalbuminemia is a classic sign of advanced disease because the liver produces less albumin, and low albumin is also associated with malnutrition and poor prognosis [N2-R3][N2-R4]. The patient’s albumin of **2.1 g/dL** is well below the normal range and fits the expected pattern in cirrhosis [N2-R3][N2-R4]. This low albumin level also supports the diagnosis of an advanced cirrhosis state and may reflect both hepatic dysfunction and protein malnutrition [N2-R3].

Anemia is also likely present. The patient’s **RBC 3.9** and **HGB 11.2** are low enough to suggest anemia, and anemia is common in cirrhosis. The evidence states that anemic patients with cirrhosis have been reported to have higher MELD scores and lower albumin levels, which reinforces the idea that anemia and cirrhosis are closely linked in this patient [N2-R1]. Additionally, Healthline notes that people with anemia are also more likely to have lower albumin levels, further supporting the interpretation that anemia contributes to the low albumin and is a clinically meaningful finding in cirrhosis [N2-R2]. 

Together, these values suggest anemia and malnutrition as plausible explanations for the low albumin. The low albumin is particularly important because it indicates impaired liver synthetic function and is associated with worse outcomes in cirrhosis [N2-R3][N2-R4]. The evidence also supports that lower albumin levels may reflect liver failure rather than a simple nutritional deficiency, especially in the context of cirrhosis [N2-R4].

### Whether further labs are needed

Based on the current results, further labs are reasonable. The evidence does not provide a complete lab panel, so it would be prudent to check for **MELD score components** such as creatinine, bilirubin, and INR, as well as **coagulopathy markers** and **electrolytes**, especially sodium and potassium, since cirrhosis can affect these. The evidence also suggests that malnutrition and hepatic failure are central concerns in cirrhosis, which may prompt additional workup for protein status, nutritional deficiency, and complications of advanced liver disease [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4]. Because the provided information is limited, the safest interpretation is that **further labs are needed** to fully assess the patient’s cirrhosis severity and guide management [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4].

### Summary
- **Albumin 2.1** suggests advanced cirrhosis and poor hepatic synthetic function [N2-R3][N2-R4].
- **Anemia** is likely and associated with lower albumin and worse cirrhosis severity [N2-R1][N2-R2].
- **Further labs** are needed to assess MELD, coagulation, electrolytes, and nutritional status [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4].

## Lactulose and confusion management decision-making

### Should lactulose be reduced, held, or continued?

The evidence strongly supports continuing lactulose in the current setting. Lactulose and rifaximin are standards of care for the prevention of overt hepatic encephalopathy in patients with cirrhosis [N3-R1][N3-R2]. In acute hepatic encephalopathy, lactulose is usually given until encephalopathy begins to improve, and once acute encephalopathy is resolved, it is targeted at **2–3 bowel movements per day** [N3-F1]. This means lactulose is generally **continued rather than reduced or held** unless there is a specific reason to modify it.

### How lactulose might affect confusion

Lactulose is used to reduce ammonia production and lower blood ammonia levels, which is the core mechanism in hepatic encephalopathy [N3-F1]. The evidence explains that lactulose lowers stool pH, increases colonic acidification, and promotes the formation of nonabsorbable NH₄⁺, which reduces plasma ammonia concentrations [N3-F1]. This mechanism is directly tied to improving or preventing confusion in cirrhosis because hepatic encephalopathy is associated with mental status changes, including confusion [N1-R4][N6-F3].

Lactulose also increases bowel movements and fecal nitrogen excretion, which further helps reduce ammonia absorption [N3-F1]. The evidence also notes that lactulose is associated with side effects such as diarrhea, flatulence, bloating, and perianal irritation, but it remains the “gold standard” for acute hepatic encephalopathy [N3-F1]. In this patient, the recent confusion suggests that hepatic encephalopathy may be a contributing factor, so continuing lactulose is likely appropriate.

### Caveats and alternative explanations for confusion

There are important caveats:
1. **Lactulose can cause diarrhea**, which may worsen electrolyte disturbances and electrolyte imbalance in cirrhosis [N3-F1]. This is especially important in a patient with advanced cirrhosis, ascites, and minimal pedal edema, because electrolyte disturbances can exacerbate confusion [N3-F1][N5-R2].
2. **Confusion in cirrhosis may have other causes**: the evidence explicitly says that confusion should be evaluated for acute precipitants such as infections, GI bleeding, medications, and dehydration [N3-F1]. The patient’s recent confusion must be considered in that context.
3. **Confusion may reflect hepatic encephalopathy or other acute processes**: the evidence notes that confusion is a presenting symptom of hepatic encephalopathy and that it may be confused with delirium or other acute neurological states [N6-F3]. The patient’s recent confusion should not be assumed to be solely due to cirrhosis without ruling out other causes.

### Bottom line
In this patient, **lactulose should generally be continued rather than reduced or held**, because it is a standard therapy for hepatic encephalopathy and is associated with improved ammonia control and mental status [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F1]. However, the decision should be made cautiously, keeping in mind that **confusion may have other causes** and that **lactulose-related side effects** could affect the patient’s tolerance and electrolyte status [N3-F1][N6-F3].

## Progress-note structure and drafting guidance

### Standard elements of an inpatient progress note for cirrhosis
The evidence supports a structured progress note that includes:
- **Patient summary/condition status**
- **Significant events since admission**
- **Interventions and treatments**
- **Labs and vitals**
- **Medications**
- **History and complications**
- **Assessment and plan**
- **Documentation of mental status changes**
- **Mention of cirrhosis complications**
- **Discussion of precipitating factors and next steps** [N4-R1][N4-R4][N4-R5][N4-F2]

The Connect Care Cirrhosis Care Path explicitly includes standardized note templates, documentation supports, and standardized problem overviews, and it emphasizes structured data entry for symptoms, signs, labs, procedures, medications, scores, and calculators [N4-F2]. This means the note should be organized around the patient’s cirrhosis-specific features and should track progress in a goal-directed way.

### How to summarize labs, vitals, meds, and history
The note should summarize the patient’s current **labs**, **vitals**, **medications**, and **history** clearly and concisely. For labs, the evidence supports including albumin, hemoglobin, RBC count, and any other relevant cirrhosis-related tests [N2-R3][N2-R4]. For vitals, temperature, BP, HR, and any abnormal findings should be recorded [N4-R4]. For medications, the note should list the current medications, especially **lactulose**, **beta-blocker**, and any other relevant medications [N4-R1][N4-R4]. For history, the note should summarize advanced cirrhosis, **variceal bleed**, **ascites**, **minimal pedal edema**, and the patient’s **stable mental status now** versus **recent confusion** [N4-F2][N5-R2][N5-R3][N6-F3].

### How to document the decision to adjust lactulose or hold it
The decision to continue lactulose should be documented as part of the **assessment and plan**. The evidence supports continuing lactulose in cirrhosis, especially in patients with hepatic encephalopathy or recent confusion, and it should be targeted at **2–3 bowel movements per day** after acute encephalopathy resolves [N3-F1]. The note should also note the **reason for the decision**, such as:
- recent confusion
- need to manage hepatic encephalopathy
- ongoing cirrhosis complications
- caution about side effects and electrolyte risk [N3-F1][N6-F3]

The note should also include a discussion of **caveats**, such as the risk of diarrhea and electrolyte disturbances, and whether further evaluation of the cause of confusion is needed [N3-F1][N6-F3].

### Bottom line
A good inpatient progress note for this patient should include:
1. A clear patient summary of cirrhosis and complications [N4-F2].
2. A concise summary of labs, vitals, meds, and history [N4-R1][N4-R4].
3. A discussion of recent confusion and the role of hepatic encephalopathy [N1-R4][N6-F3].
4. A decision to continue lactulose with a rationale and caveats [N3-F1][N6-F3].
5. A plan that addresses ascites, variceal bleed, and any other relevant management steps [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R5].
